topics.title: Urinary Incontinence: Causes, Risks & the Five Types
topics.summary: Urinary incontinence is urine leaking when the client does not mean to void. It is a symptom, not normal aging, and comes in five types.
objectives: You can define urinary incontinence and explain why it is a symptom, not a disease.
You can explain the pressure contest between the bladder and the urethra.
You can name the risk factors and say why each one raises risk.
You can teach prevention, including why clients should not cut their fluids.
You can tell stress, urge, reflex, overflow, and functional incontinence apart.
topics.bigPicture:
Urinary incontinence (UI) means urine leaks out when the person did not mean to let it go. Some clients leak when they laugh. Others cannot reach the bathroom in time. Many feel ashamed, stop going out, and never tell anyone.

Hold on to two ideas. First, UI is a symptom, not a disease. Something is causing it, so your job is to ask why. Second, UI is not a normal part of aging. It is common in older adults, but common is not normal, and treatments exist. Once you know the five types, you can match each client's story to the right type and the right plan.
recap: UI is involuntary urination. It is a symptom of poor bladder control, never a normal part of aging.
Leaking happens when bladder pressure is higher than urethral pressure.
Three slide causes: diuretics (more urine), pregnancy (uterus presses down), and low estrogen after menopause (weak urethra).
Do not cut fluids. Teach more than 2,000 mL/day, spaced out, with less at night.
Stress = leaks with cough, sneeze, or lift. Urge = strong sudden urge, can't hold it.
Reflex = nerve damage, leaks with NO urge. Overflow = full bladder that dribbles. Functional = can't get there in time.
A dribbling client with a firm, full bladder may have retention. Assess and empty the bladder, not just change pads.

keyTerms.def: Urine that leaks out without the person meaning to void. It is a sign of poor bladder control, not a disease on its own.
The muscle in the bladder wall. It relaxes while the bladder fills and squeezes to push urine out.
The squeeze of the urethra and its sphincter muscles that holds urine in. When it weakens, urine escapes more easily.
A sling of muscles at the bottom of the pelvis. It holds up the bladder, uterus, and rectum and helps close the urethra.
Bladder prolapse. The bladder sags down into the wall of the vagina.
Urethral prolapse. The urethra sags down into the wall of the vagina.
Waking up at night to urinate.
A prostate that has grown larger but is not cancer. It can squeeze the urethra and block urine flow in males.
Things that irritate the bladder lining and cause urgency: alcohol, caffeine, artificial sweeteners, and acidic or spicy foods.
Nerve stimulation used to change how the nerves that control the bladder fire.
Transurethral resection of the prostate. Surgery done through the urethra that removes extra prostate tissue so urine can flow.

sections.heading: What is urinary incontinence?
sections.keyIdea: UI is a symptom of a bladder-control problem, so the nurse looks for the cause instead of just keeping the client dry.
sections.body:
UI is involuntary urination. That means urine comes out when the client did not choose to void. It is a sign that bladder control is impaired. Something is wrong with the muscles, the nerves, the bladder, or the client's ability to reach a toilet.

Because UI is a symptom, the treatment depends on the cause. Weak pelvic muscles after childbirth need a different plan than an enlarged prostate or dementia. That is why the five types matter.

UI harms the body and the mind. Wet skin breaks down and gets rashes and infections. Clients may fall while rushing to the bathroom at night. Many feel shame, avoid friends, stop exercise and intimacy, and become isolated or depressed. UI is especially common in long-term acute care residents.
sections.example: Mrs. A, 78, wears a pad 'just in case.' She has stopped going to church because she fears leaking. She says, 'My mother had this too. It's just old age.' The nurse gently explains that leaking is common but not normal with aging. It has causes that can be found, and many treatments help. The nurse reports the problem so it can be evaluated, instead of simply handing out more pads.

sections.heading: Why does urine leak?
sections.keyIdea: Urine leaks whenever bladder pressure becomes stronger than the urethra's squeeze.
sections.body:
Think of it as a pressure contest. The bladder pushes outward as it fills or squeezes. The urethra and pelvic floor squeeze to hold urine in. Normally the urethra wins until the person decides to void.

Leaking happens when the bladder side gets stronger, the urethra side gets weaker, or both. Your slides name three causes.
bullets: Diuretics ('water pills') make the kidneys produce more urine fast. The bladder fills quickly and pressure rises.
Pregnancy: the growing uterus presses down on the bladder and raises its pressure.
Low estrogen after menopause: estrogen keeps urethral and vaginal tissue thick and firm. Without it, the tissue thins, and the urethra cannot seal as well.
sections.analogy: Picture a water balloon with your fingers pinching the neck closed. The balloon is the bladder. Your pinch is the urethra. Squeeze the balloon harder, or loosen your pinch, and water squirts out. Every type of incontinence is some version of that.

check.q: A client just started furosemide (a diuretic) and now leaks on the way to the bathroom. Why?
check.a: The diuretic makes more urine quickly. The bladder fills fast, and its pressure rises above what the urethra can hold back before the client reaches the toilet.

sections.heading: Who is at risk, and why?
sections.keyIdea: Most risk factors either add pressure on the bladder, weaken the urethra, or make it harder to reach the toilet.
sections.body: Learn the reason behind each risk factor. Then you can remember the list and explain it to the client. Tip: if a diuretic causes urgency, the usual fix is a morning dose and easy bathroom access. Do not skip doses or cut fluids.

rows: Age
The bladder holds less, pelvic muscles weaken, and nerve control declines. UI is still not 'normal.'
Female sex
A shorter urethra, plus pregnancy, childbirth, and menopause, weaken the support around the bladder.
Homebound or long-term care resident
More trouble moving, more memory problems, and more need for help to reach the toilet.
Obesity
Extra belly weight presses on the bladder all the time.
Smoking
A chronic cough pounds the pelvic floor, and nicotine irritates the bladder.
Diabetes
High glucose pulls extra water into the urine. Nerve damage can dull bladder feeling and emptying.
Inactivity
Weak muscles, including the pelvic floor, and slower trips to the bathroom.
Pregnancy
Hormone changes plus the weight of the uterus on the bladder.
Depression
Low energy for toileting and self-care. It also often follows UI.
Constipation
A rectum full of hard stool presses on the bladder and urethra.
UTI
Infection irritates the bladder wall and causes urgency and frequency.
Bladder irritants
Caffeine, alcohol, artificial sweeteners, and acidic or spicy foods trigger bladder squeezes.
Diuretics and sedatives
Diuretics make more urine. Sedatives dull the feeling of a full bladder and slow the client's response.

sections.example: An older client got a sleeping pill at night and also takes an evening diuretic. At 0300 the bed is wet. The diuretic filled the bladder. The sedative kept the client from noticing and waking in time. The nurse reports the pattern, asks about moving the diuretic to the morning, and plans toileting before bed and during the night.

sections.heading: How can clients prevent leaking?
sections.keyIdea: Teach healthy habits and plenty of fluid, because cutting fluids makes urine concentrated and irritates the bladder.
sections.body:
Your slides (Box 5.3) list lifestyle changes that prevent UI. Many clients make one big mistake. They drink less, thinking less in means less leaking. It backfires.

Concentrated urine irritates the bladder lining. The detrusor then squeezes more often, which means more urgency and more leaking. Low fluid also raises the risk of UTI and constipation, and both cause UI. The smart plan is to space fluids through the day and cut back mainly in the evening.
bullets: Reach a healthy weight, exercise, and stop smoking.
Eat a high-fiber diet to prevent constipation, which presses on the bladder.
Avoid bladder irritants: alcohol, caffeine, artificial sweeteners, and acidic or spicy foods.
Drink enough: more than 2,000 mL/day, spaced throughout the day. Do NOT limit fluids.
Limit fluids at night to prevent nocturia.
steps: Less fluid in
Urine becomes more concentrated
The bladder wall gets irritated
More bladder squeezes, so more urgency and more leaking
sections.analogy: Concentrated urine is like extra-strong coffee. A little of it has a big kick. Dilute urine is gentle on the bladder lining.

check.q: A client with urge incontinence says, 'I stopped drinking water after lunch so I won't leak.' What do you teach?
check.a: Cutting fluid makes urine concentrated, which irritates the bladder and can worsen urgency. Drink more than 2,000 mL/day spread through the day. Cut back mainly in the evening, and avoid caffeine and alcohol.

sections.heading: The five types at a glance
sections.keyIdea: To find the type, ask two questions: what triggers the leak, and does the client feel it coming?
sections.body: Your slides name five types: stress, urge, reflex, overflow, and functional. Use this table as your map. The next two sections explain each type in plain words.

rows: Stress
Relaxed pelvic muscles and a weak urethra lower urethral resistance. Extra pressure comes from pregnancy, obesity, a cystocele, or a urethrocele.
Leaks with sneezing, coughing, or lifting; uncontrollable leaking
Lifestyle changes, behavior therapy, Kegels, estrogen, pessary, urethral insert, surgery
Urge
Overactive detrusor raises bladder pressure; the client cannot stop voiding
Strong, sudden urge and can't hold it; nocturia
Lifestyle changes, behavior therapy, Kegels, anticholinergic and estrogen medicines
Reflex
Detrusor spasms from nerve damage or tissue damage (MS, spinal cord injury)
Voids with NO urge; sudden, unexpected loss
Medicine for the underlying condition, neuromodulation, catheterization (risk vs. benefit), surgery
Overflow
Blocked outlet or weak detrusor; the bladder overfills and pressure rises
Leaking or dribbling from a full bladder; UTIs
Medication, catheterization, surgery (for example, TURP for an enlarged prostate)
Functional
The bladder works, but the response to the need is impaired (dementia, disability, poor mobility)
Can't reach the toilet in time
Catheterization, absorbent briefs, home changes, PT/OT, assistive devices, easy clothing

sections.heading: Stress vs. urge: strain or sudden urge?
sections.keyIdea: Stress incontinence leaks with physical strain; urge incontinence leaks after a strong, sudden need to go.
sections.body:
Stress incontinence has nothing to do with emotional stress. 'Stress' means physical strain on the belly. The pelvic muscles have relaxed and the urethra is weak, so urethral resistance is low. Pregnancy, obesity, a cystocele, or a urethrocele add pressure and push urine past the weak seal. The client leaks a small amount with a sneeze, cough, laugh, or lift.

Treatment strengthens or supports the seal. Options include Kegels, estrogen, a pessary or urethral insert, behavior therapy, and surgery.

Urge incontinence is the 'gotta go NOW' type. The detrusor is overactive. It squeezes when it should rest, so the client cannot hold it once the urge hits. Nocturia is common. Treatment includes cutting irritants, bladder training, Kegels, and medicines: anticholinergics to calm the detrusor, and estrogen.

Some clients have both types. This is mixed incontinence, so always ask about both triggers.
sections.example: Ms. K, 45, a mother of three, leaks a little when she jumps on the trampoline or sneezes. That is stress incontinence, so Kegels are first-line teaching. Mr. P, 70, says, 'When I have to go, I have to go. I barely make it, and I'm up three times a night.' That is urge incontinence with nocturia. Expect bladder training, less caffeine, and maybe an anticholinergic.

sections.heading: Reflex, overflow, and functional types
sections.keyIdea: Reflex has no warning, overflow is a full bladder spilling over, and functional is a trip-to-the-toilet problem.
sections.body:
Reflex incontinence comes from the nerves. Multiple sclerosis (MS) or a spinal cord injury interrupts messages between the bladder and brain. The detrusor spasms on its own. The client voids with no urge and no warning. Catheters are weighed on risk versus benefit, because they drain the bladder but raise infection risk.

Overflow incontinence is the full-bucket type. Either the outlet is blocked or the detrusor is too weak to empty. Causes include retention, kidney stones (calculi), and BPH. The bladder overfills and urine dribbles out. Stagnant urine grows bacteria, so UTIs are common. Overflow is really retention in disguise.

Functional incontinence means the urinary system may work fine. The client cannot recognize the need, cannot get there, or cannot manage clothing. Causes include dementia, physical disability, and poor mobility. Fix the access: a bedside commode, a clear lit path, a raised toilet seat, grab bars, a walker, PT/OT, and clothing with elastic waists or Velcro.
sections.analogy: Overflow is like a sink with a clogged drain and the faucet running. The water spills over the edge. Mopping the floor (more pads) does not fix the clog.
sections.example: Mr. J, 74, has BPH. He dribbles all day, has had two UTIs this year, and his bladder feels firm above the pubic bone. That is overflow, so expect a bladder scan and catheterization, and maybe medicine or a TURP. Mrs. L, 82, has dementia and uses a walker. She stays dry when staff walk her to the toilet every 2 hours. She is wet when she tries alone at night. That is functional, so the fix is access and scheduled help.

check.q: A client with a spinal cord injury suddenly finds himself wet without feeling any urge. Which type is this?
check.a: Reflex incontinence. Nerve damage causes detrusor spasms, so urine is lost suddenly with no urge.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Most wrong answers come from mixing up look-alike types or treating the wetness instead of the cause.
sections.body: These pairs look alike on exam questions. Use the right column to tell them apart.

rows: Stress vs. urge
Stress leaks with strain (cough, sneeze, lift). Urge leaks after a strong, sudden need to void.
Urge vs. reflex
Urge: the client feels it coming but can't hold it. Reflex: no urge at all, usually with nerve damage.
Overflow vs. 'just incontinent'
Overflow has a firm, full bladder and constant dribbling. Scan and empty the bladder before using pads.
Functional vs. bladder problem
In functional UI the bladder works. The barrier is getting there: mobility, vision, memory, or help.
Chronic UI vs. new sudden UI
New, sudden leaking with burning, fever, or confusion in an older adult points to an acute cause such as UTI. Report it.
'Drink less' vs. 'space fluids'
Never cut total fluid. Space it out and reduce it in the evening.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect questions that ask you to name the type from a story or choose the safest first action.
sections.body:
Common patterns: match a client story to a type, choose correct teaching, or spot retention hiding as incontinence. SATA (select all that apply) items often cover risk factors or prevention.

Sample: A 76-year-old man with BPH says he 'leaks all day' and never feels empty. His lower abdomen is firm above the pubic bone. What should the nurse do first? (A) Apply an absorbent brief. (B) Perform a bladder scan. (C) Teach him to limit fluids. (D) Teach Kegel exercises.
steps: Read the stem: an older man with BPH, constant leaking, a feeling of not emptying, and a firm lower abdomen.
What is it really asking? Which action addresses the most dangerous problem first.
Key cues: BPH plus dribbling plus a firm bladder points to overflow from retention.
Why the others are wrong: a brief only hides the problem. Limiting fluids concentrates urine and raises UTI risk. Kegels help stress incontinence, not a blocked outlet.
The answer is B. A bladder scan confirms how much urine is retained so the bladder can be emptied.
Reusable strategy: when a leaking client has a full bladder, assess and empty the bladder before managing the wetness.

sections.heading: Worked case: night wetting on the unit
sections.keyIdea: Look for every cause of new leaking: medicines, timing, and barriers to reaching the toilet.
sections.body: Mr. D, 81, was admitted with pneumonia. He was dry at home. Now he is wet most nights. He takes furosemide at 2000 and got a sedative for sleep. He uses a walker, has poor vision, and his call light is often out of reach. His urine is clear, and he has no burning or fever.
steps: Recognize cues: new night wetting, evening diuretic, sedative, walker, poor vision, call light out of reach.
Rule out an acute cause: no burning, fever, or cloudy urine, so UTI is less likely. Check his bladder for fullness to rule out retention.
Name the type: mostly functional. His bladder works, but he can't get to the toilet in time.
Act: ask the provider about moving the diuretic to the morning. Report the sedative's effect.
Remove barriers: bedside commode or urinal, night-light, clear path, glasses within reach, call light at hand.
Offer toileting before bed and on a schedule at night. Evaluate: fewer wet episodes and intact skin.

check.q: Should the nurse tell Mr. D to stop drinking after supper?
check.a: He can drink less in the evening, but his total intake should not drop. Limiting fluids concentrates urine, irritates the bladder, and raises UTI and constipation risk.

mnemonics.name: The five trigger words
mnemonics.text: STRESS = sneeze, cough, lift. URGE = 'gotta go NOW.' REFLEX = no warning, nerve damage. OVERFLOW = full bucket dribbles. FUNCTIONAL = can't get there in time.

pearls: 'Stress' incontinence means physical strain (cough, sneeze, lift), not emotional stress.
Urge = feels it coming but can't hold it. Reflex = does NOT feel it coming at all.
Overflow is really retention. A wet client with a firm, full bladder needs the bladder emptied, not just a pad.
Never teach a client with UI to cut fluids. Teach more than 2,000 mL/day, spaced out, with less in the evening.
Functional incontinence is often fixed by the environment: commode, night-light, clear path, and easy clothing.
redFlags: Constant dribbling with a firm, distended bladder above the pubic bone: suspect overflow from retention. Scan the bladder and notify the provider.
New, sudden incontinence with burning, urgency, fever, or acute confusion in an older adult: suspect UTI or another acute cause and report it.
A client with BPH who cannot void and has lower belly pain: acute retention. This outranks routine incontinence care.

checks.q: Why is UI called 'a symptom, not a disease,' and how does that change nursing care?
checks.a: It is caused by something else, such as weak muscles, an overactive detrusor, nerve damage, a blockage, or mobility limits. The nurse looks for and reports the cause and type, not just the wetness.

checks.q: A postmenopausal client asks why she started leaking after menopause. What is the explanation?
checks.a: Lower estrogen thins and weakens the urethral tissue, so the urethra cannot seal as tightly against bladder pressure.

checks.q: Match each client to a type: (a) leaks when she laughs, (b) has Alzheimer disease and can't find the bathroom, (c) a man with BPH who dribbles constantly.
checks.a: (a) Stress, (b) functional, (c) overflow.

checks.q: Which two medicine classes on the risk slide add to incontinence, and how?
checks.a: Diuretics make more urine. Sedatives dull the feeling of a full bladder and slow the client's response.

checks.q: Why is a client with overflow incontinence prone to UTIs?
checks.a: The bladder never fully empties, so urine sits still and bacteria multiply.

topics.title: Managing Incontinence: Kegels, Training, Devices & Meds
topics.summary: Most incontinence improves with nurse teaching: Kegels and bladder retraining first, then devices and medicines, then surgery, adapted to the client's age.
objectives: You can teach Kegel exercises with the correct timing.
You can tell bladder training, habit training, and scheduled toileting apart and match each to a client.
You can describe the devices for women and the catheter options for overflow incontinence.
You can give the key nursing points for anticholinergics, topical estrogen, and BPH smooth-muscle relaxers.
You can apply lifespan points for bed-wetting children, pregnancy, and older adults.
topics.bigPicture:
Good news: much urinary incontinence can get better. A lot of that improvement comes from what the nurse teaches. Before anyone reaches for a pill or surgery, clients learn to strengthen the pelvic floor, retrain the bladder, and change habits.

Think of treatment as a ladder. The bottom rungs are lifestyle changes and behavior therapies. The middle rungs are devices and medicines. The top rung is surgery. Your job is to know what each rung does, which type of UI it fits, and what to watch for. Then you adapt the plan to the client's age and situation.
recap: Kegels: find the muscles, squeeze 3–10 seconds, relax 10–15 seconds, repeat 10 times. Do them with an empty bladder.
Bladder training stretches the time between voids toward every 3–4 hours. Habit training follows the diary. Scheduled toileting uses fixed times.
Devices for women: pessary, urethral insert, bladder support. Catheters are for overflow from retention or neurogenic bladder.
Anticholinergics (oxybutynin) calm the bladder but cause the 'dries.' Avoid them in glaucoma.
BPH smooth-muscle relaxers can drop blood pressure. Teach the client to rise slowly.
Surgery: cystocele or urethrocele repair, prostatectomy, artificial sphincter, urethral sling.
Enuresis: primary = never dry; secondary = dry 6+ months, then wet again. Bed-wetting alarms work best.

keyTerms.def: Pelvic floor muscle exercises. They improve muscle tone around the bladder and rectum.
Slowly lengthening the time between voids, toward every 3–4 hours, while holding off urges. It steadies an overactive bladder.
Voiding at the times the client's own bladder diary shows leaks usually happen, to get ahead of them.
Taking the client to the toilet at fixed times, such as every 2 hours, whether or not they feel the urge.
A record of when and how much the client drinks and voids, and when leaks happen.
A device, often ring-shaped, placed in the vagina to hold up the bladder neck and pelvic organs.
A small plug placed in the female urethra to stop leaks. It is removed to void.
'In and out' catheter use. The catheter drains the bladder and is removed right away.
A catheter placed through the lower belly wall directly into the bladder.
A medicine that blocks acetylcholine and relaxes the detrusor, reducing urgency and frequency. Example: oxybutynin (Ditropan).
A medicine that makes the bladder squeeze to promote voiding. Example: bethanechol (Urecholine). Used for retention.
Thin, dry, inflamed vaginal and urethral tissue caused by low estrogen after menopause.
Involuntary urination, usually bed-wetting at night, in a child old enough to be dry.

sections.heading: What is the treatment ladder?
sections.keyIdea: Start with teaching and behavior changes, then move to devices and medicines, and use surgery last.
sections.body:
Treatment climbs a ladder. Each rung adds more risk and cost, so start low.

A catheter is never the first answer just to keep a client dry. It carries infection risk. Match each treatment to the type of incontinence and its cause.
bullets: Bottom rung: lifestyle changes and behavior therapy (Kegels, bladder training, habit training, scheduled toileting).
Middle rungs: devices (pessary, urethral insert, catheters) and medicines.
Top rung: surgery, when the lower rungs have not worked.

sections.heading: How do you teach Kegel exercises?
sections.keyIdea: Find the right muscles first, then squeeze 3–10 seconds, relax 10–15 seconds, and repeat 10 times.
sections.body:
Kegels strengthen the pelvic floor. They improve muscle tone for both the bladder and the rectum. Stronger muscles squeeze the urethra closed. They help stress incontinence most. They also help urge incontinence, because a quick squeeze can calm an urge, and they help fecal incontinence.

The hardest part is finding the muscles. Your slides (Box 5.4) give two ways. They are the muscles used to stop the flow of urine and to hold in a bowel movement or gas.
steps: Tighten the pelvic floor muscles.
Hold the squeeze for 3–10 seconds.
Relax for 10–15 seconds.
Repeat 10 times.
bullets: Stopping the stream is only for finding the muscles. Do the exercises with an empty bladder, not while voiding.
Keep breathing. Keep the belly, thighs, and buttocks relaxed. Only the pelvic floor works.
Results take weeks of regular practice, so encourage the client to keep going.
sections.analogy: Kegels are like bicep curls for a muscle no one can see. One workout does nothing. Weeks of steady practice build a stronger drawstring around the urethra and anus.

check.q: A client asks, 'So I should stop and start my urine every time I go?' How do you respond?
check.a: No. Stopping the stream once helps you find the muscles. Do the exercise with an empty bladder: squeeze 3–10 seconds, relax 10–15 seconds, repeat 10 times.

sections.heading: Which bladder retraining fits which client?
sections.keyIdea: Bladder training stretches the time between voids, habit training follows the diary, and scheduled toileting follows the clock.
sections.body:
Your slides (Box 5.5) list behavior therapies that sound alike. Focus on the goal of each.

Bladder training is for the overactive bladder. It starts with a bladder diary. The client then lengthens the time between voids, slowly working toward every 3–4 hours. When an urge comes early, the client holds it off with quick Kegels, slow breathing, and staying still. This steadies the bladder and reduces urgency and frequency. It needs an alert, motivated client. Your textbook shows a sample schedule (p. 337).

Habit training uses the diary differently. If leaks happen around 1000 and 1400, the client toilets a little before then. Scheduled toileting means fixed times, such as every 2 hours, urge or not. It fits clients with dementia. Lifestyle changes support all of these.

rows: Bladder training
Slowly lengthen time between voids (goal every 3–4 hours); hold off urges; keep a diary
Urge incontinence or frequency in an alert, motivated client
Habit training
Void at the times the diary shows leaks usually happen
Clients with a predictable leak pattern
Scheduled toileting
Toilet at fixed, regular times
Clients with dementia or who depend on others (functional UI)

sections.example: Mrs. T voids every 45 minutes 'just in case' and still leaks with sudden urges. The nurse starts bladder training. This week she waits 1 hour between voids. She uses quick Kegels and slow breathing to ride out urges. Then she adds 15 minutes each week toward a 3–4 hour goal. At her next visit she is at 2 hours. That is progress, so the plan continues.

check.q: A resident with moderate dementia is wet several times a day. Which therapy fits, and why not bladder training?
check.a: Scheduled toileting at fixed times. Bladder training needs the client to remember, delay, and hold off urges, which a client with dementia usually can't do.

sections.heading: What devices and catheters help?
sections.keyIdea: Devices for women support the urethra; catheters are for a bladder that does not empty, not for convenience.
sections.body:
Your slides list three devices for women. All are inserted.

Catheters are listed for overflow incontinence from retention or a neurogenic bladder, where the bladder does not empty. Use them only when the benefit clearly outweighs the infection risk.

For any indwelling catheter, keep the drainage bag below the bladder and off the floor, so urine cannot flow back. Keep tubing free of kinks, secure the catheter, and clean the insertion site daily.
bullets: Pessary: goes in the vagina and holds up the bladder neck and pelvic organs. It helps stress incontinence and a cystocele.
Urethral insert: a small plug in the urethra that stops leaks during activity. It is removed to void.
Bladder support: devices in the vagina that support the bladder neck.
Intermittent ('in and out') catheter: drains the bladder on a schedule, then comes out. Lower infection risk than a catheter left in. Many clients learn to do it themselves.
Indwelling or suprapubic catheter: stays in to drain all the time. Indwelling goes through the urethra. Suprapubic goes through the belly wall.
sections.analogy: A pessary is like a bracket put back under a sagging shelf. It does not change the shelf. It props it up so things stay in place.
sections.example: Mr. R has MS and overflow incontinence because his bladder does not empty. The team teaches him intermittent self-catheterization every few hours. He washes his hands, inserts the catheter, drains the bladder, and removes it. He stays dry, empties fully, and has a lower infection risk than with an indwelling catheter.

sections.heading: Which medicines treat incontinence?
sections.keyIdea: Anticholinergics calm an overactive bladder but dry everything out; cholinergics do the opposite and are used for retention.
sections.body:
Your slides (Medications 5.1 and 5.3) list these drugs. Learn why each is used and the main safety point.

Do not mix up two opposites. An anticholinergic such as oxybutynin (Ditropan) reduces bladder squeezes for urge incontinence. A cholinergic such as bethanechol (Urecholine) makes the bladder squeeze. It is used for retention, not urge incontinence.

Anticholinergics cause the 'dries': dry mouth, hard stools, and a bladder that holds urine. If a client on one stops voiding and has belly discomfort, suspect retention and assess the bladder first.

rows: Anticholinergics (oxybutynin [Ditropan])
Relax the overactive detrusor; less urgency and frequency; treat urge incontinence
Significant side effects: dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, confusion in older adults. Avoid in glaucoma.
Topical estrogen
Postmenopausal women with atrophic vaginitis; rebuilds thin tissue so the urethra seals better
Applied locally (cream or ring); teach correct use
BPH smooth-muscle relaxers
Relax muscle at the bladder neck and prostate so urine flows out more easily
Watch for low BP. Teach to rise slowly; dizziness can cause falls.
UTI medicines (antibiotics)
Infection irritates the bladder and causes urgency and leaking
Finish the full course; push fluids unless restricted
Urinary antispasmodic (mirabegron [Myrbetriq])
Relaxes the bladder to reduce urgency (concept slides)
Slides warn of significant side effects; monitor BP

sections.example: Mrs. B, 79, started oxybutynin two weeks ago. Her leaking is better. Today her mouth is 'dry as cotton,' she has had no bowel movement in four days, and her daughter says she seems more forgetful. These are classic anticholinergic effects. The nurse checks for a full bladder, encourages fluids and fiber, and reports the constipation and new confusion to the provider.

check.q: An older client with glaucoma has a new order for oxybutynin. What should the nurse do?
check.a: Question the order and notify the provider. Anticholinergics like oxybutynin should be avoided in glaucoma because they can raise eye pressure.

sections.heading: What surgeries are options?
sections.keyIdea: When conservative care fails, surgery repairs, lifts, or replaces the structures that keep urine in.
sections.body: Your slides list these surgeries. Each one fixes a specific problem.
bullets: Cystocele repair: lifts and supports a bladder that has sagged into the vaginal wall.
Urethrocele repair: does the same for a sagging urethra.
Prostatectomy: removes all or part of the prostate to relieve a blockage in males. TURP is one approach.
Artificial sphincter: an implanted cuff around the urethra that the client opens to void.
Urethral sling: a strip of mesh or tissue under the urethra, like a hammock. It keeps the urethra closed during coughing or lifting. Common for stress incontinence.

sections.heading: What about children who wet the bed?
sections.keyIdea: Night bed-wetting is not a problem until after age 7, and a bed-wetting alarm is the most effective treatment.
sections.body:
Enuresis is involuntary urination, usually at night, in a child old enough to be dry. Most children gain control between 2 and 5 years. Daytime control comes before nighttime control. Night wetting is not considered a problem until after age 7. It is more common in deep sleepers. Daytime wetting in an older child may signal a problem and needs a closer look.

Understanding why the child wets is key to the outcome and to the child's well-being. Most often, it is not caused by a medical disorder.
bullets: Primary enuresis: the child has never been dry at night.
Secondary enuresis: the child was dry at night for at least 6 months, then started wetting again. Look for a trigger: stress, illness, UTI, or constipation.
Treatment: behavior changes, diet changes to manage constipation, and sometimes medicine.
Bed-wetting alarms are the most effective treatment. Most children outgrow it as they mature.
Secondary enuresis with heavy thirst, frequent urination, or weight loss needs prompt evaluation, not just reassurance.
sections.example: An 8-year-old was dry for a year and now wets the bed again. That is secondary enuresis. The nurse asks about new stress, such as a new sibling or school, plus constipation and UTI signs. The nurse explains it is usually not caused by disease and is not the child's fault. The nurse discourages punishment and explains that an alarm works best.

sections.heading: Pregnancy and the older adult
sections.keyIdea: Teach Kegels in pregnancy; for older adults, remove the barriers that keep them from reaching the toilet.
sections.body:
Pregnancy raises risk in three ways. Hormones relax supporting tissue. The growing uterus presses on the bladder. Delivery can injure or weaken the pelvic floor. Your slides stress Kegels during pregnancy. Also teach the client to avoid irritants and not to limit fluids.

In the older adult, many barriers are outside the bladder. Your slides list limited mobility, poor vision, dementia, lack of access to a toilet, no help, and privacy concerns. The body also changes. The bladder holds less, more urine is left after voiding, more urine is made at night, and pelvic muscles weaken.

Care focuses on access and dignity. Answer call lights fast. Keep the path clear and lit. Place a bedside commode. Keep glasses in reach. Offer toileting on a schedule, and give privacy.

check.q: An older client with poor vision and a walker is wet mainly at night. Name three nursing changes.
check.a: Any three: night-light and clear path, commode or urinal within reach, glasses at the bedside, scheduled offers of help, fast call-light response, and privacy.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Match the treatment to the cause, and watch for medicines that create a new problem.
sections.body: These look-alikes cause many wrong answers.

rows: Bladder training vs. habit training
Bladder training stretches the interval toward 3–4 hours. Habit training times voids to the client's own diary pattern.
Habit training vs. scheduled toileting
Habit training follows the diary. Scheduled toileting follows fixed clock times and fits dementia.
Anticholinergic vs. cholinergic
Anticholinergic (oxybutynin) calms the bladder for urge UI. Cholinergic (bethanechol) makes it squeeze for retention.
Pessary vs. urethral insert
Pessary goes in the vagina and supports the bladder neck. Insert goes in the urethra and is removed to void.
Catheter for retention vs. for dryness
Catheters treat a bladder that won't empty. They are not used just to keep a client dry.
Primary vs. secondary enuresis
Primary: never dry at night. Secondary: dry 6+ months, then wet again. Find the trigger.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Questions test correct teaching, matching the therapy to the client, and medicine safety.
sections.body:
Expect questions on Kegel timing, choosing a retraining method, and spotting side effects. Watch for low BP after a BPH relaxer, and retention or confusion after an anticholinergic. Evaluation items ask whether a goal is met. Progress means continue the plan.

Sample: A client on oxybutynin for urge incontinence has not voided in 8 hours and reports lower belly discomfort. What should the nurse do first? (A) Give the next dose. (B) Encourage more oral fluids. (C) Assess the bladder with a bladder scan. (D) Teach Kegel exercises.
steps: Read the stem: an anticholinergic, no voiding for 8 hours, and lower belly discomfort.
What is it really asking? What is the likely problem, and what is the first action?
Key cues: anticholinergics can cause urinary retention. Discomfort plus no output suggests a full bladder.
Why the others are wrong: another dose worsens retention. More fluid adds to a bladder that can't empty. Kegels do not empty a full bladder.
The answer is C. Assess first. The scan confirms retention so the provider can be notified and the bladder emptied.
Reusable strategy: when a new medicine could cause the symptom, hold off on more drug and assess first.

sections.heading: Worked case: a new mother who leaks
sections.keyIdea: Choose the lowest rung that fits the cause, and teach it clearly.
sections.body: Ms. V, 32, is 6 weeks postpartum after her second vaginal birth. She leaks a little when she coughs or picks up her toddler. She has no burning or urgency. She has started drinking less water so she will leak less.
steps: Recognize cues: leaks with coughing and lifting, recent vaginal births, no urgency or UTI signs.
Name the type: stress incontinence from a weakened pelvic floor.
Choose the lowest rung: Kegel exercises and lifestyle teaching.
Teach Kegels: find the muscles, then squeeze 3–10 seconds, relax 10–15 seconds, repeat 10 times, with an empty bladder.
Correct the fluid mistake: drink more than 2,000 mL/day, spaced out, with less at night. Avoid irritants.
Evaluate in a few weeks: fewer leaks with coughing and lifting. If not better, devices or other options can be discussed.

check.q: Ms. V asks if she should practice by stopping her urine stream every time she voids. What do you say?
check.a: No. Stopping the stream once helps find the muscles. Do the exercises with an empty bladder, because stopping the stream often can interfere with full emptying.

mnemonics.name: Kegel '3-10, 10-15, times 10'
mnemonics.text: Squeeze 3–10 seconds, relax 10–15 seconds, repeat 10 times.

pearls: Behavior therapy and Kegels come before drugs or surgery.
Bladder training = stretch the interval (toward 3–4 hours). Habit training = follow the diary. Scheduled toileting = fixed clock times.
Anticholinergics calm the bladder but dry everything out. Avoid in glaucoma. Watch older adults for confusion, constipation, and retention.
BPH smooth-muscle relaxers can drop BP, so teach the client to change positions slowly.
redFlags: New confusion, a full bladder, or no urine output after starting an anticholinergic: suspect side effects and retention. Hold the next dose and notify the provider.
Dizziness or a near-fall after a BPH smooth-muscle relaxer: a low-BP safety priority. Keep the client safe and report it.
Secondary enuresis with burning, frequent urination, heavy thirst, or signs of distress at home: report it for evaluation (UTI, diabetes, or stress or abuse).

checks.q: What is the difference between bladder training and habit training?
checks.a: Bladder training slowly lengthens the time between voids toward 3–4 hours and teaches urge control. Habit training has the client void at the times the diary shows leaks usually happen.

checks.q: Which type of incontinence are catheters listed for?
checks.a: Overflow incontinence from urinary retention or a neurogenic bladder.

checks.q: A client on a BPH smooth-muscle relaxer feels lightheaded getting out of bed. Why, and what do you teach?
checks.a: The drug can lower blood pressure. Teach the client to sit on the edge of the bed first, rise slowly, and call for help if dizzy.

checks.q: A 6-year-old who has never been dry at night wets the bed. Primary or secondary, and is it a concern yet?
checks.a: Primary enuresis. Night wetting is not considered a problem until after age 7, and most children outgrow it.

checks.q: Why is topical estrogen used for some postmenopausal women with UI?
checks.a: Low estrogen causes thin, weak tissue (atrophic vaginitis). Topical estrogen rebuilds the tissue, so the urethra resists leaks better.

topics.title: Urinary Retention & Promoting Normal Voiding
topics.summary: Urinary retention means the bladder cannot empty. Acute retention is a painful emergency; chronic retention is quiet incomplete emptying. Nurses assess, decompress, promote voiding, and prevent infection.
objectives: You can tell acute retention (an emergency) from chronic retention.
You can assess the bladder by palpation, percussion, bladder scan, and post-void residual.
You can name the risk factors for retention and explain why each one causes it.
You can help a client void naturally before a catheter is considered.
You can teach catheter care, protect the skin, and prevent UTIs.
You can apply lifespan points for children, postpartum clients, and older adults.
topics.bigPicture:
Incontinence is urine coming out when it shouldn't. Urinary retention is the opposite. Urine won't come out when it should. Your slides define it as the inability to empty the bladder.

Retention matters because a full bladder causes pain. It stretches and damages the bladder wall, breeds infection, and can push urine back toward the kidneys. It also hides behind other problems. The client who dribbles all day may have a full bladder. The restless post-op client may simply need to void. You will see retention after surgery, after childbirth, and in older men with an enlarged prostate.
recap: Retention is inability to empty the bladder. Acute = sudden, painful, can't void, an emergency. Chronic = voids but never fully empties.
Acute signs: firm, distended bladder above the pubic bone with dullness on percussion. Confirm with a bladder scan.
Chronic signs: painless, hard to start, weak stream, frequency, still feels full after voiding.
Risks: anesthesia, brain or spinal cord injury, anticholinergics, antihistamines, constipation, repeated UTIs, stones, weak detrusor, enlarged prostate.
First priority in acute retention is bladder decompression by catheter. Then treat the cause.
Try natural voiding first: usual position, privacy, time, running water, warm bedpan, prompt help.
Expected urine output is about 0.5 mL/kg/hr. Low output with a full bladder means retention.

keyTerms.def: Being unable to empty the bladder, either completely (acute) or partly (chronic).
A sudden, painful inability to void even though the bladder is full. A medical emergency.
The client can urinate but cannot fully empty the bladder. It is usually painless.
The urine left in the bladder right after the client voids. It is measured by bladder scan or catheter.
A handheld ultrasound that estimates how much urine is in the bladder. It does not enter the body.
Draining an overfull bladder, usually with a catheter.
Tapping on the body to hear the sound underneath. A full bladder sounds dull, not hollow.
Pressing firmly downward over the lower belly, above the pubic bone, to help push urine out.
A catheter placed through the belly wall above the pubic bone straight into the bladder.
The strength of the bladder's muscle wall. Poor tone means a weak squeeze that can't empty the bladder.
A drug that makes the bladder squeeze to promote voiding. Example: bethanechol (Urecholine).
Urine flowing backward from the bladder up toward the kidneys.

sections.heading: Acute vs. chronic: which kind is it?
sections.keyIdea: Acute retention is sudden, painful, and an emergency; chronic retention is painless and easy to miss.
sections.body:
Acute retention is a sudden, painful inability to void even though the bladder is full. The client badly needs to go and can't. Your slides call this a medical emergency. The bladder can overstretch and be injured, pain is severe, and pressure can back up to the kidneys.

Chronic retention means the client can urinate but can't fully empty. It develops slowly and is often painless. The leftover urine sits still and grows bacteria.

rows: Sudden, painful inability to void
Painless
Firm, distended bladder
Hard to start or keep the stream going
Dullness on percussion over the bladder
Weak flow
Emergency: decompress the bladder
Frequency (small amounts often) and urgency after voiding

sections.analogy: Acute retention is a water balloon filled to bursting with the knot tied shut. Chronic retention is a bathtub drain that only half works. Some water goes down, but a puddle always stays at the bottom and gets stale.

check.q: A man voids 50 mL every 30 minutes, says he 'never feels empty,' and has a weak stream but no pain. Acute or chronic?
check.a: Chronic retention. He can void but doesn't empty fully: frequency, weak flow, urgency after voiding, and no pain.

sections.heading: How do you assess the bladder?
sections.keyIdea: Feel for a firm bladder above the pubic bone, tap for dullness, and confirm the amount with a bladder scan.
sections.body:
An empty bladder sits low in the pelvis and can't be felt. A full one rises above the pubic bone. Use these steps.

If a client with an indwelling catheter has no drainage and lower belly discomfort, check the simple things first. Look for a kinked or squeezed tube, or a bag that is not hanging below the bladder.
bullets: Palpate (feel) the lower belly. A full bladder feels firm, round, and distended. The client may wince.
Percuss (tap) over it. You hear dullness, the flat sound of fluid, instead of the hollow sound of bowel.
Bladder scan: a handheld ultrasound that estimates the volume.
Post-void residual (PVR): have the client void, then scan right away. A healthy bladder leaves very little, often under about 50 mL.
A large residual means the bladder is not emptying. Follow your facility's threshold for when to catheterize or call the provider.
sections.example: Mr. W had knee surgery under spinal anesthesia this morning. Eight hours later he has not voided despite 1,500 mL of IV fluid. He is restless. His lower belly is firm and dull above the pubic bone. The nurse does a bladder scan, which shows a large volume. This is acute retention after anesthesia. The nurse notifies the provider and expects an order to catheterize.

sections.heading: Output, I&O, and the 24-hour urine
sections.keyIdea: Compare output with the expected 0.5 mL/kg/hr; low output plus a full bladder means urine is made but not released.
sections.body:
Always compare intake with output. A client who is drinking or getting IV fluids but voiding little needs a bladder check.

The concept slides give expected output as 0.5 mL/kg/hr, about 30 mL/hr on average. A 70-kg adult should make about 35 mL/hr, or about 280 mL over 8 hours. Low output with a large residual is retention, not kidney failure. The kidneys are making urine. It just isn't getting out.

Assistive personnel can measure and record output. Bladder assessment, teaching, and decisions about catheterizing stay with the RN.

Sometimes the provider orders a 24-hour urine, such as a creatinine clearance test. Follow these steps.
steps: Have the client void, discard that first urine, and note the time. It was made before the test began.
Save every void for the next 24 hours.
End with a final void at the same clock time, and save it.
Keep the container cold or on ice per lab instructions.
If any void is thrown away, notify the lab and restart the collection.

check.q: A 60-kg client voided 90 mL in 8 hours. Is that enough?
check.a: No. Expected is 0.5 mL/kg/hr, or 30 mL/hr, so about 240 mL in 8 hours. Assess the bladder. A full bladder points to retention.

sections.heading: Why does the bladder stop emptying?
sections.keyIdea: Retention happens when the nerve signal fails, the bladder muscle is too weak, or the outlet is blocked.
sections.body: Group the slide risk factors by how they work. Then you can reason through any new drug or condition.

rows: Nerve signal disrupted
Anesthesia; brain or spinal cord trauma
Anesthesia blocks the feeling of fullness and the urge to void. Injury cuts the brain–bladder pathway.
Medicines that relax the bladder
Anticholinergics; antihistamines (such as diphenhydramine)
They block acetylcholine, the signal that makes the detrusor squeeze.
Weak squeeze
Poor detrusor muscle tone
The bladder can't make enough pressure to empty.
Outlet blocked or pressed on
Enlarged prostate; kidney stones; constipation
The prostate squeezes the urethra. Stones block flow. A full rectum presses on the bladder neck.
Infection and scarring
Repeated UTIs
Swelling and scars interfere with emptying, and leftover urine invites more infection.

bullets: The same drug that calms an overactive bladder (oxybutynin) can cause retention, especially in older men with BPH.
A man with an enlarged prostate should avoid antihistamines and other anticholinergic drugs.
A fecal impaction can cause retention. Check the bowels when a client can't empty the bladder.

check.q: An older man with BPH took an over-the-counter antihistamine for a cold and now can't void. Why?
check.a: Antihistamines have anticholinergic effects that weaken the bladder squeeze. His prostate already narrows the outlet. Together they caused acute retention.

sections.heading: How is retention treated?
sections.keyIdea: First relieve the pressure by draining the bladder, then fix whatever caused the retention.
sections.body:
In acute retention, the first priority is bladder decompression by catheter. Draining the urine relieves pain and protects the bladder and kidneys. Then the team treats the cause.

The concept slides also list a cholinergic drug, bethanechol (Urecholine). It makes the detrusor squeeze to promote voiding. It is for a weak bladder with an open outlet, not a blockage. It is working when the client voids well with a small residual. It can raise liver and pancreatic enzyme levels, so report rising values. Think of it as the opposite of an anticholinergic.
bullets: Antibiotics when a UTI is present.
Resection of the prostate (such as TURP) for a blocking enlarged prostate.
Removal of calculi (stones) that block the outflow.
Repair of a cystocele or rectocele, where a sagging bladder or rectum kinks the outflow.
Suprapubic catheter for long-term drainage when the urethra can't be used.

sections.heading: How do you help a client void naturally?
sections.keyIdea: Use the client's usual position, privacy, time, and gentle cues before anyone reaches for a catheter.
sections.body:
Your slides (Box 5.6) aim to promote independence and normal toileting. The sphincter must relax to let urine out, and anxiety tightens it. So comfort and privacy really matter.

A client who has to 'hold it' while waiting for help can overstretch the bladder and lose the urge. Answer call lights promptly and offer toileting regularly.
bullets: Position: help the client into their usual voiding position. This also raises belly pressure to push urine out. Most women sit or squat. Many men void best standing, so help a man stand with a urinal if it is safe and allowed.
Relaxation: give privacy (close the door and curtain) and enough time without rushing.
Sensory cues: run water in the sink, pour warm water over the perineum, or place the client's hand in warm water.
Timing: prevent delays by giving help quickly.
Bed-bound client: use a warm bedpan (cold makes muscles tense). Sit the client upright with hips and knees flexed.

check.q: A post-op client on bed rest says, 'I just can't go in this bedpan.' Name three things to try before a catheter.
check.a: Any three: warm the bedpan; raise the head of the bed with hips and knees flexed; give privacy and time; run water or pour warm water over the perineum; check if a bedside commode is allowed.

sections.heading: Credé, catheters, skin, and UTI prevention
sections.keyIdea: Use Credé only when ordered for an open outlet, teach catheter care, keep skin dry, and prevent infection.
sections.body:
The Credé maneuver means pressing firmly down over the bladder, just above the pubic bone, to push urine out. It is for a weak bladder with an open outlet, such as a neurogenic bladder. Use it only when it is in the care plan.

Never use it when the outlet is blocked or urine flows backward toward the kidneys. Pressing on a bladder that can't drain forward pushes urine up to the kidneys.

Skin: urine breaks down into ammonia, which irritates skin. Clients who dribble need prompt cleansing, drying, and a moisture barrier.

UTI prevention: retained urine and catheters are the two biggest risks. Ensure full emptying, encourage fluids unless restricted, give perineal care, use aseptic technique, and remove catheters as soon as possible.
bullets: Home catheter teaching: keep the bag below the bladder.
Keep the tubing free of kinks, and secure the catheter to the thigh.
Wash hands before handling it, and clean around the catheter daily.
Drink enough fluids.
Report fever, cloudy or foul urine, flank pain, or no drainage.
sections.analogy: Urine left on skin is like a wet diaper left on a baby. As it sits, it turns to ammonia. That harsh smell is the same chemical that burns the skin.

sections.heading: Retention across the lifespan
sections.keyIdea: Watch children with weak streams, check every postpartum bladder, and expect more leftover urine in older adults.
sections.body:
Children: your slides list physical or congenital deformities of the urinary tract, and circumcision or genital mutilation. These can cause infection and scarring that narrows the outlet. A child who strains, has a weak stream, or keeps getting UTIs needs evaluation.

Pregnancy and birth: risks include cesarean delivery (anesthesia and catheter use), birth trauma (swelling around the urethra), and urogynecology surgery. Postpartum clients are at risk for overdistention and residual urine, and urine output rises early after birth. A full bladder pushes the uterus up and to one side. Help postpartum clients void early and often.

Older adults: the aging bladder is more fibrous. It holds less and leaves more residual urine. Older men with an enlarged prostate are at highest risk.
sections.example: Six hours after a vaginal birth with a large tear, a new mother has not voided. Her fundus sits high and to the right of the midline. Her lower belly bulges. The nurse helps her to the toilet, runs water, and pours warm water over the perineum. If she still can't void, the nurse does a bladder scan and catheterizes per protocol.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Retention often looks like something else, so check the bladder before you treat the behavior or the wetness.
sections.body: These look-alikes are common on exams.

rows: Low output: retention vs. kidney failure
Retention has a full bladder and a large residual. The urine is made but not released.
Restless post-op client: pain or anxiety vs. full bladder
High intake, little output, and a firm lower belly mean check the bladder first.
Dribbling: incontinence vs. overflow
Constant dribbling with a palpable bladder is retention with overflow until proven otherwise.
Bethanechol vs. oxybutynin
Bethanechol makes the bladder squeeze (retention). Oxybutynin calms it (urge UI) and can cause retention.
Credé: open outlet vs. blocked outlet
Credé helps a weak bladder with an open outlet. Never use it for a blockage or reflux.
Catheter not draining: retention vs. tube problem
Check for kinks and bag position first.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect priority questions where acute retention outranks stable problems, plus assessment and teaching items.
sections.body:
Common patterns: pick the client to see first, spot retention from cues, choose natural voiding steps, and delegate safely. Acute, painful retention outranks chronic retention and stable output.

Sample: Which client should the nurse see first? (A) A man with BPH who has a weak stream and voids often. (B) A client who has not voided for 10 hours and has severe lower belly pain. (C) A client with an indwelling catheter draining clear yellow urine. (D) A postpartum client who voided 400 mL an hour ago.
steps: Read the stem: four clients with bladder issues; choose who needs the nurse first.
What is it really asking? Which client is unstable or at risk of harm now?
Key cues: 10 hours with no voiding plus severe pain means acute retention, an emergency.
Why the others are wrong: A is chronic retention and stable. C is draining normally. D has voided a good amount.
The answer is B. Assess with a bladder scan and prepare for decompression.
Reusable strategy: sudden, painful, and 'can't' beat slow, painless, and 'can.'

sections.heading: Worked case: the restless hip patient
sections.keyIdea: When a post-op client is restless, check the bladder before you treat the behavior.
sections.body: Mrs. E, 79, is 10 hours out from hip surgery with spinal anesthesia. She got 1,800 mL IV and has voided 60 mL. She is restless and keeps pulling at her gown. She takes oxybutynin at home. Her lower belly is firm.
steps: Recognize cues: anesthesia, an anticholinergic, high intake, very low output, restlessness, and a firm lower belly.
Analyze: three retention risks plus signs of a full bladder. Restlessness may be bladder pain.
Assess: palpate, percuss for dullness, and do a bladder scan.
Act: notify the provider and expect an order to catheterize (decompress).
Try natural steps if time allows: privacy, a warm bedpan, upright with hips and knees flexed, running water.
Evaluate: after draining, she is calm, and her bladder is soft and not distended.

check.q: Should the nurse give Mrs. E a PRN sedative for restlessness first?
check.a: No. Assess the bladder first. Her restlessness is likely from a full bladder, and a sedative would hide the cue and could worsen retention.

pearls: Acute retention (sudden, painful, full bladder, can't void) is an emergency. Decompress the bladder.
Chronic retention is sneaky: painless, weak stream, frequency, and still feels full after voiding.
Anticholinergics and antihistamines cause retention. Check the med list of any client who suddenly can't void.
Palpate for a firm bladder, percuss for dullness, then confirm with a bladder scan.
Try natural methods first: privacy, time, usual position, warm bedpan, running water, warm water over the perineum.
redFlags: Sudden, painful inability to void with a firm, distended bladder: acute retention. Scan, notify the provider, and prepare to catheterize.
A post-op or postpartum client with no voiding for hours, restlessness, and a full bladder: act now. Do not wait for shift change.
A client with a catheter who has fever, cloudy foul urine, or flank pain: suspect a catheter-associated UTI and report it promptly.

checks.q: Why is acute urinary retention a medical emergency?
checks.a: The bladder is full and the client can't void. It causes severe pain, can overstretch and damage the bladder, and pressure can back up to the kidneys. It must be decompressed promptly.

checks.q: What percussion finding suggests retention?
checks.a: Dullness above the pubic bone, the flat sound of a fluid-filled bladder.

checks.q: Name two medicine classes on the slides that raise retention risk.
checks.a: Anticholinergics and antihistamines.

checks.q: Why does the nurse cleanse and protect the skin of a client who dribbles urine?
checks.a: Urine breaks down into ammonia, which irritates and breaks down skin. Prompt cleansing, drying, and a barrier protect it.

checks.q: A male client can't void lying in bed. He is allowed to stand. What is the best first step?
checks.a: Help him stand at the bedside with a urinal, and give privacy and time. His usual position raises belly pressure to help him void.

topics.title: Constipation & Fecal Impaction
topics.summary: Constipation is infrequent or hard-to-pass stool. Left alone, stool can harden into an impaction. Fiber, fluid, activity, routine, and careful laxative use prevent and treat it.
objectives: You can explain why slow-moving stool gets hard and how constipation becomes an impaction.
You can name the risk factors, including the five constipating medicine groups.
You can recognize constipation, the Rome IV criteria, and the classic signs of impaction.
You can teach fiber, fluid, and bowel routine, and remove an impaction safely.
You can use laxatives and enemas safely and know when not to use them.
You can apply lifespan points for children, pregnancy, and older adults.
topics.bigPicture:
Everyone gets constipated sometimes, so it is easy to shrug off. In nursing it is not minor. It is common in clients who are in the hospital, immobile, older, or taking opioids. It can turn into a fecal impaction, a mass of stool so hard and stuck that it can damage the bowel wall.

The key idea is time. The colon's job is to absorb water from stool. The longer stool sits, the more water is pulled out, and the harder and drier it gets. Almost everything in this lesson is about keeping stool moving or getting stuck stool out safely.
recap: Constipation = fewer than 3 BMs per week or hard-to-pass stool. Slow transit lets more water be absorbed, so stool gets hard.
Impaction = a hard mass in the rectum or colon. It can cause ulceration, perforation, poor blood flow, and urinary retention.
Constipating medicines: opioids, iron, antihistamines, antacids, and antidepressants.
Liquid, foul-smelling seepage with no formed stool in a constipated client = impaction until proven otherwise. No antidiarrheal.
Fiber goal: 25 g/day for women, 38 g/day for men, always with enough fluid.
During manual removal, watch for a vasovagal response (slow pulse, low BP, fainting). Stop if it happens.
Laxatives: avoid long-term use and for simple constipation. Never give them when a blockage is suspected.
Encopresis in a child: treat the constipation, and always consider abuse.

keyTerms.def: Fewer than 3 bowel movements a week, or stool that is hard to pass. Stool is often dry and hard.
A mass of hardened stool stuck in the folds of the rectum or colon that the client can't pass.
A hard, packed mass in the GI tract. Your slides use it to describe impacted stool 'hard as concrete.'
The wave-like squeezing of the bowel that moves stool along.
Standard symptom criteria used to diagnose chronic constipation.
A medicine that promotes a bowel movement, for example by pulling water into stool or stimulating the bowel.
An osmotic laxative that holds water in the stool to soften it.
An enema of saline, mineral oil, and glycerin for severe constipation or impaction.
A large-volume enema of milk and molasses that stimulates the bowel to empty hard stool.
Gently breaking up impacted stool with a gloved, lubricated finger and removing it.
A reflex from vagus nerve stimulation. The heart slows and blood pressure drops, causing dizziness or fainting.
Repeated soiling with stool by a child who should already have bowel control, usually from constipation and withholding.
The natural urge to have a bowel movement after eating, strongest after breakfast.

sections.heading: What is constipation, and how does impaction form?
sections.keyIdea: The longer stool sits in the colon, the more water is pulled out, until it may become a stuck, rock-hard mass.
sections.body:
Your slides define constipation as fewer bowel movements or difficult passage of stool. The concept slides add a number: fewer than 3 BMs per week. Stool is dry and hard. The client strains and feels they have not fully emptied.

Why does stool get hard? The colon absorbs water. Slow movement allows more water to be absorbed. Hard stool hurts to pass, so the client delays, and the cycle repeats.

'Normal' varies from 3 times a day to 3 times a week. Constipation is a change from the client's usual pattern. If it goes on, it can become a fecal impaction. Follow the chain below.
steps: Stool is kept in the colon, and water keeps being removed.
It hardens into a mass the client can't pass, like a bezoar, 'hard as concrete.'
Pressure inside the colon rises.
The pressure can cause ulcers, perforation (a hole), and poor blood flow to the bowel wall.
The mass presses on the bladder neck and urethra and can cause urinary retention.
sections.analogy: Think of the colon as a long sponge-lined tube. Stool that moves quickly stays moist. Stool that lingers gets wrung out again and again, until it is as hard as clay left in the sun.

check.q: A client says, 'I go every three days, but it's soft and easy.' Is this constipation?
check.a: Not necessarily. Normal varies. If this is her usual pattern and stool passes easily without straining, it is her normal.

sections.heading: Who is at risk, and why?
sections.keyIdea: Most risk factors either slow the gut or make the client delay going.
sections.body: Your slides list these risk factors. Ask yourself whether each one slows the bowel or makes the client ignore the urge.

rows: Activity
Too little activity, immobility
Movement stirs peristalsis. Bed rest slows the gut.
Habits and routine
Irregular habits, changes in routine, lack of privacy
Delaying the urge (busy day, shared room, bedpan) lets stool dry out, and the urge fades.
Overuse of aids
Long-term laxative or enema use
The bowel becomes dependent, and normal reflexes weaken.
GI conditions
IBS, pelvic floor problems, slow gastric movement
The bowel moves stool slowly or can't coordinate pushing it out.
Population
Older adults, women
Slower gut, less activity, more medicines; hormone effects.
Medicines
Opioids, iron, antihistamines, antacids, antidepressants
Opioids and anticholinergic-type drugs slow peristalsis. Iron and some antacids harden stool.
Mental health
Anxiety, depression
They change gut movement and lower activity, appetite, and self-care.

sections.example: Mr. G, 68, is on day 3 after hip surgery. He takes oxycodone every 4 hours and started iron for blood loss. He has barely left bed, shares a room, and has had no BM since admission. His risks: opioids, iron, immobility, no privacy, and older age. The nurse expects a bowel plan, encourages fluid and fiber, gets him walking, and offers private toileting after breakfast.

check.q: Name the five medicine groups on the constipation risk slide.
check.a: Opioids, iron, antihistamines, antacids, and antidepressants.

sections.heading: Constipation or impaction: how can you tell?
sections.keyIdea: Liquid, foul-smelling seepage with no formed stool in a constipated client means impaction, not diarrhea.
sections.body:
A constipated client normally does not have loose stool. Your slides say loose stools are atypical without laxatives. So when liquid appears, think impaction. Liquid stool from higher in the colon seeps around the hard mass.

This is a classic trap. Staff see liquid stool, call it 'diarrhea,' and give an antidiarrheal. That makes the impaction worse. Instead, ask when the last formed BM was, examine the abdomen, and do a rectal exam per policy.

For chronic constipation, your slides use the Rome IV criteria. The client needs 2 or more of the Rome IV signs listed after the table. Symptoms must be present for the last 3 months (at least 12 weeks), starting at least 6 months before diagnosis.

rows: BMs less often than normal (fewer than 3 per week)
Liquid, foul-smelling seepage with no formed stool
Straining; hard, dry stools
Rectal pain
Frequent gas, belly discomfort, and distention
Repeated urges and straining with nothing passed
Poor appetite; decreased bowel sounds
Anorexia (no appetite), distention, and cramping
The client feels 'ill'
Nausea and vomiting

bullets: Straining
Lumpy or hard stool
A feeling of not fully emptying
Needing manual help (such as a finger) to pass stool
Fewer than 3 BMs per week
sections.example: Mrs. H, 85, in long-term care, has had no formed BM in 8 days. The aide reports 'diarrhea': small amounts of foul-smelling brown liquid all day. She is not eating, and her belly is distended. This is impaction with seepage. The nurse holds any antidiarrheal, assesses the abdomen, and notifies the provider.
sections.analogy: An impaction is like a boulder in a stream. The water can't push it out, so it trickles around the edges. The trickle doesn't mean the stream is flowing well. It means something is blocking it.

check.q: Why is an antidiarrheal harmful for liquid seepage around an impaction?
check.a: The liquid is leaking around a hard mass. Slowing the bowel worsens the impaction and raises colon pressure, increasing the risk of ulcers or perforation.

sections.heading: How do fiber, fluid, and routine help?
sections.keyIdea: Fiber with plenty of fluid, activity, and a regular unhurried toilet time keep stool soft and moving.
sections.body:
Teaching comes first. Your slides cite Box 5.7 for diet and Box 5.8 for behavior.

Fiber: 25 grams per day for women and 38 grams per day for men. Good sources are whole-grain cereals and bread, fresh fruit, and vegetables. Add fiber slowly to limit gas and bloating.

Fluid: fiber works by holding water in stool. Fiber without enough fluid can make constipation worse. If fiber goes up and constipation gets worse, check fluid intake first.

Routine: the goal is a BM on a regular schedule. Prevention from your slides is simple: fiber, fluids, exercise, don't ignore the urge, and don't overuse laxatives.
bullets: Sit upright on a toilet or commode, lean slightly forward, and support the feet. A footstool raises the knees and straightens the rectum.
Respond to the urge. Toilet after meals, especially breakfast, to use the gastrocolic reflex.
Give privacy, relaxation, and unhurried time.
Use abdominal massage to stimulate movement.
Encourage regular activity, such as walking.

check.q: A client doubled her fiber but is more constipated. What do you check first?
check.a: Her fluid intake. Fiber needs water. Without enough fluid, it can harden stool and worsen constipation.

sections.heading: How do you remove an impaction safely?
sections.keyIdea: Break the stool up gently, follow with an enema or suppository, and watch the pulse for a vasovagal response.
sections.body:
Manual removal is used when an impaction won't pass. Many facilities require a provider order, so follow policy. Disimpaction stays with the nurse. It is not delegated to assistive personnel.

Stimulating the rectum can trigger the vagus nerve. This is a vasovagal response. It causes a slow heart rate, low blood pressure, dizziness, sweating, or fainting.
steps: Check the order and policy. Take a baseline pulse.
With a gloved, lubricated finger, gently break the impaction into smaller pieces.
Remove the pieces, and check the pulse throughout.
Stop at once if the heart rate drops or the client feels faint.
Follow with an enema or suppository, as ordered, to finish emptying.

check.q: During disimpaction, the client's pulse drops from 78 to 48, and he feels faint. What do you do?
check.a: This is a vasovagal response. Stop the procedure, keep him lying flat, monitor vital signs, and notify the provider.

sections.heading: When are laxatives and enemas safe?
sections.keyIdea: Use laxatives carefully and briefly, and never when a bowel blockage is suspected.
sections.body:
Your slides give three laxative rules. Before any PRN laxative, check the bowel history and abdomen. Vomiting, distention, and no gas suggest a blockage. Report it instead of giving a laxative.

For opioid-induced constipation, a stool softener alone usually is not enough. Expect a stimulant laxative such as senna to be added.
bullets: Avoid long-term use. The bowel becomes dependent.
Avoid for simple constipation. Laxatives interfere with normal bowel reflexes. Try fiber, fluid, activity, and routine first.
Never use with a blockage or obstruction. Forcing the bowel against a blockage can cause perforation.

rows: Miralax (polyethylene glycol)
Osmotic laxative that holds water in stool to soften it
Mix in a full glass of liquid; may take 1–3 days to work
Milk and molasses enema
Large-volume enema that stimulates emptying
For stubborn constipation or impaction; give per order and protocol
SMOG enema
Saline, Mineral Oil, Glycerin
Softens, lubricates, and stimulates; for severe constipation or impaction
Stool softeners
Let water mix into stool so it passes more easily
Often paired with opioids, but a stimulant such as senna is usually added

sections.example: A client takes a stimulant laxative every night 'to stay regular.' The concept slides warn that laxative use blocks natural reflexes and may cause constipation instead of relieving it. The nurse teaches fiber, fluids, activity, and responding to the urge. The nurse works with the provider on a plan to taper. A change in bowel habits lasting weeks should be referred to the primary care provider.

sections.heading: Children and encopresis
sections.keyIdea: Painful stools make children hold stool, which makes the next stool worse; break the cycle without punishment.
sections.body:
Infants normally have several BMs a day. Stool may change when breast milk is switched to formula. A color or texture change alone is not constipation.

Your slides diagnose constipation in a child over 4 years, toilet trained, with symptoms for 1 month, and at least 2 of the bullets below. Causes can be physical (malformations, disease) or psychologic.

The classic cycle is withholding. One painful BM makes the child hold stool. It dries and grows, so the next BM hurts more. Children who are 'too busy' playing also ignore the urge. Treat with a toilet routine after meals, fiber, fluids, activity, behavior changes, and laxatives when ordered. Never punish.

Encopresis is repeated soiling by a child who should have bowel control. Liquid stool leaks around a large retained mass. Signs include withholding, small hard painful BMs, withdrawal, and stress. Care includes family teaching, emotional support, medicine, fiber, behavior plans, and teachers (bathroom access at school). Always consider abuse.
bullets: 2 or fewer stools per week
At least 1 episode of fecal incontinence per week
Excessive stool withholding
Painful, hard BMs
A large mass in the rectum
Very large stools that clog the toilet

check.q: A 7-year-old has started soiling at school, has small, hard, painful BMs, and seems withdrawn. What fits, and what else must the nurse consider?
check.a: Encopresis. Besides treating the constipation and involving family and teachers, the nurse must consider abuse. Safety comes first.

sections.heading: Pregnancy and older adults
sections.keyIdea: Pregnancy slows the gut through the uterus, progesterone, and iron; older adults need teaching that a daily BM is not required.
sections.body:
Pregnancy: the growing uterus pushes the small intestine aside and slows movement. Higher progesterone relaxes smooth muscle. Prenatal vitamins with iron harden stool. Straining leads to hemorrhoids. Teach fiber, fluids, and activity, and to report hemorrhoid pain or bleeding. Involve the provider instead of telling her to stop the vitamin.

Older adults: constipation affects 24–50%. Causes include poor general health, more medicines, less activity, poor teeth, little fresh produce or fiber, and drinking less to avoid leaks or from low thirst. Cutting fluid to prevent bladder leaks causes constipation, and constipation worsens urinary problems.

Your slides also name perceived constipation, the belief that you must have a BM every day. These clients may overuse laxatives and create real dependence. Teach that normal ranges from 3 times a day to 3 times a week. In an older adult who can't report symptoms, new agitation and poor appetite with no stool for days call for a bowel assessment.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: The biggest trap is calling impaction seepage 'diarrhea'; the next is giving a laxative into a blockage.
sections.body: Use this table to separate look-alikes.

rows: Diarrhea vs. impaction seepage
Seepage is liquid, foul, with no formed stool in a client with constipation risks. Check for impaction first.
Simple constipation vs. obstruction
Vomiting, distention, and no gas suggest blockage. No laxatives. Report it.
More fiber vs. more fiber plus fluid
Fiber without water hardens stool. Always pair them.
Stool softener vs. stimulant for opioids
A softener alone usually fails. Expect senna or another stimulant.
Daily BM 'needed' vs. normal range
Normal is 3 a day to 3 a week. Daily laxatives backfire.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect questions that hide an impaction behind 'diarrhea' and ask for the first action.
sections.body:
Common patterns: spot impaction, choose teaching on fiber and fluid, pick safe disimpaction steps, and know when a laxative is unsafe. Delegation items: assistive personnel can help with scheduled toileting and privacy. Assessment, teaching, and disimpaction stay with the nurse.

Sample: A client on opioids and iron has had no formed stool for 6 days. Today he has small amounts of foul liquid stool. What should the nurse do first? (A) Give the PRN loperamide (an antidiarrheal). (B) Assess for fecal impaction. (C) Collect a stool culture. (D) Restrict oral fluids.
steps: Read the stem: opioids, iron, 6 days with no formed stool, and now liquid stool.
What is it really asking? Is this true diarrhea or something hiding behind it?
Key cues: two constipating drugs, no formed stool, and liquid seepage point to impaction.
Why the others are wrong: loperamide slows the bowel and worsens impaction. A culture fits infection, not this pattern. Cutting fluids hardens stool more.
The answer is B. Assess: last formed BM, abdomen, and rectal exam per policy.
Reusable strategy: when a finding doesn't fit the history, assess for the hidden cause before treating the symptom.

sections.heading: Worked case: the quiet nursing home resident
sections.keyIdea: In a client who can't report symptoms, behavior changes may be the only sign of a bowel problem.
sections.body: Mr. F, 88, has dementia and lives in long-term care. He takes an antidepressant and an antacid. For two days he has been agitated and eating little. His chart shows no BM for 5 days. His belly is distended, and he grimaces when it is touched.
steps: Recognize cues: no BM for 5 days, two constipating medicines, agitation, poor appetite, distention.
Analyze: he can't report pain, so agitation may be his way of showing discomfort. Suspect constipation or impaction.
Assess first: bowel sounds, belly exam, last formed stool, and a rectal exam per policy. Check for a full bladder too.
Act: report to the provider. If impacted, expect manual removal with pulse checks, then an enema or suppository.
Prevent: fiber and fluid, toileting after breakfast with feet supported, more activity, and a medicine review.
Evaluate: soft, formed stool on a regular schedule and calmer behavior.
