check.q: Mr. F's family asks for a daily laxative 'so this never happens again.' What do you teach?
check.a: Long-term laxatives make the bowel dependent and weaken reflexes. Fiber, fluid, activity, and a regular toilet time are safer. Any medicine plan is set with the provider.

mnemonics.name: Fiber goals
mnemonics.text: Women 25, men 38 grams a day. Think 'she's 25, he's 38.'

pearls: Impaction can cause urinary retention. Treating the bowel often fixes the bladder.
Fiber needs fluid. Fiber without water can make constipation worse.
Never give laxatives when a bowel obstruction is suspected.
During manual removal, watch for a vasovagal response and stop if it occurs.
redFlags: Severe or sudden belly pain, a rigid abdomen, fever, or vomiting with an impaction: suspect perforation or obstruction. Stop laxatives and enemas, and notify the provider now.
Pulse drops and the client feels faint or sweaty during disimpaction: vasovagal response. Stop, lay flat, monitor vital signs, and report.
A child with new soiling, withdrawal, and fear around toileting: treat the constipation, but also consider abuse and follow reporting policy.

checks.q: In one sentence, why does slow-moving stool become hard?
checks.a: The colon keeps absorbing water the whole time stool sits there, so slower movement means more water removed and harder stool.

checks.q: What is the daily fiber goal for women and men? Name two good sources.
checks.a: 25 grams for women and 38 grams for men. Sources: whole-grain cereals and bread, fresh fruit, and vegetables.

checks.q: Why do the slides say to avoid laxatives for simple constipation?
checks.a: They interfere with normal bowel reflexes, and long-term use can make the bowel dependent and worsen constipation.

checks.q: Infants switched from breast milk to formula have a change in stool color. Is this constipation?
checks.a: No. A change in color or texture after switching to formula is expected and is not constipation by itself.

topics.title: Fecal Incontinence & the Bowel Nursing Process
topics.summary: Fecal incontinence is loss of control of stool or gas. It signals another problem, is not normal aging, and calls for careful assessment, skin care, and dignity.
objectives: You can define fecal incontinence and tell partial from major.
You can explain the causes, risk factors, and prevention.
You can describe the surgical options, including sugar for a swollen rectal prolapse.
You can do a focused, respectful bowel assessment.
You can write measurable goals and evaluate why a goal was not met.
topics.bigPicture:
Few problems are as embarrassing as losing control of your bowels. Clients often hide it. They wear dark clothes, stay home, skip meals before going out, and avoid friends. Your slides note it is emotionally distressing and leads to social isolation.

Like urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence is a sign of another disorder, not a disorder itself. It is common in long-term care, where 50–70% of nursing home residents have it. This lesson also walks through the nursing process for bowel problems: assess, name problems, write goals, and evaluate. Those steps work for constipation too.
recap: Fecal incontinence = loss of voluntary control of stool or gas. It is a sign of another problem, never normal aging.
Partial = can't control gas or minor soiling. Major = can't control stool of normal consistency.
Causes: neurologic (spinal cord injury), trauma, inflammatory, infection, and physiologic or cognitive (depression, confusion, dementia).
Risks: advanced age, female, smoking, high BMI. Prevention: activity, fiber, fluid, Kegels, no straining, treat the cause.
Rule out impaction with seepage before calling a client 'incontinent of liquid stool.'
Sugar on a swollen rectal prolapse shrinks it by osmosis. Sphincteroplasty repairs the sphincter. A colostomy diverts stool.
Clean skin promptly after every episode, pat dry, and apply a barrier.
Goals must be client-centered and measurable. If a goal is not met, find out why before changing the plan.

keyTerms.def: Loss of voluntary control of stool or gas through the anal sphincter.
Being unable to control gas (flatus) or prevent minor soiling.
Being unable to control stool of normal consistency.
The ring of muscles that keeps the anus closed until the person chooses to have a bowel movement.
The rectum slides down and sticks out through the anus.
Water moving across tissue toward a stronger concentration, such as sugar. It pulls fluid out of swollen tissue.
Surgery that repairs a damaged anal sphincter muscle so it can close tightly again.
A surgical opening that brings the colon out through the belly wall (a stoma). Stool drains into a pouch.
A gloved, lubricated finger checks the rectum for sphincter tone, stool, masses, and tenderness.
A small tear in the lining of the anus. It hurts, especially with bowel movements.
Swollen veins in or around the anus and rectum.
Cleaning and protecting the skin between the genitals and the anus.

sections.heading: What is fecal incontinence?
sections.keyIdea: Fecal incontinence is loss of control of stool or gas, and its severity is partial or major.
sections.body:
Your slides define fecal incontinence as the loss of voluntary control of stool or gas. Gas counts. A client who can't hold gas has a form of it.

The slides sort it by severity. In partial incontinence, the client can't control gas or prevent minor soiling (staining of underwear). In major incontinence, the client can't control stool of normal consistency.

The burden goes beyond the body. It is distressing and isolating, and caregivers may find it the hardest part of care. Fear of an accident can disable a client as much as the accidents do. It is common in older adults, but it is never a normal part of aging.
sections.example: Mr. O, 72, wears a pad 'because of gas and some staining.' He has never lost a full BM. That is partial incontinence. Mrs. N, after a stroke, passes normal formed stool in bed without knowing it. That is major incontinence. Both deserve a search for the cause, not just pads.

sections.heading: Why is bowel control lost?
sections.keyIdea: Control needs feeling, a strong sphincter, and the ability to respond; anything that interferes causes incontinence.
sections.body: Bowel control needs three things. The client must feel that the rectum is full. The sphincter must be strong enough to hold. The client must notice the urge and be able to respond. Your slides sum up the cause as interference with sensory or motor control.

rows: Neurologic
Spinal cord injury (also stroke, MS, diabetic nerve damage)
The 'rectum is full' message doesn't reach the brain, or the brain can't control the sphincter.
Trauma
Childbirth injury, anal surgery, sphincter injury
The sphincter is torn or weak and can't close tightly.
Inflammatory
Inflammatory bowel conditions
An irritated bowel moves loose stool fast with strong urgency.
Infection
Infectious diarrhea
Large amounts of liquid stool overwhelm a normal sphincter.
Physiologic or cognitive
Depression, confusion, dementia
The client may not notice or respond to the urge, or may lack motivation to toilet.

bullets: The concept slides also list masses, hemorrhoids, and a deformity of the anus.
Don't forget impaction. Liquid stool seeping around a hard mass looks like incontinence. Always ask when the last formed BM was.

check.q: A client with dementia has normal sphincter tone but passes formed stool in bed several times a day. Which cause fits, and what approach helps?
check.a: A cognitive cause: she doesn't notice or act on the urge. Scheduled toileting after meals, to use the gastrocolic reflex, plus prompting works better than sphincter exercises.

sections.heading: What raises risk, and what prevents it?
sections.keyIdea: Age, female sex, smoking, and high BMI raise risk; soft, formed stool and a strong pelvic floor prevent leaks.
sections.body:
Your slides list four risk factors. Advanced age is one, but fecal incontinence is still not a normal change of aging. Being female raises risk, because childbirth can injure the sphincter and pelvic floor. Smoking and a high BMI also raise risk. Extra belly weight presses on the pelvic floor. Dementia adds risk too.

Prevention is the bullet list below. Note that fiber helps both ways. It firms up liquid stool and softens hard stool.
bullets: Regular physical activity.
Fiber and fluid for soft, formed stool. It is easier to control than liquid stool and easier to pass than hard stool.
Kegel exercises to strengthen the pelvic floor and anal sphincter. It is the same exercise taught for the bladder.
Avoid straining, which weakens the pelvic floor over time.
Treat the underlying cause, such as an infection.
sections.analogy: Think of holding a soft ball versus holding water. You can grip a ball, but water slips through your fingers. Soft, formed stool is the easiest kind for a sphincter to hold.

sections.heading: Which procedures and surgeries help?
sections.keyIdea: Sugar shrinks a swollen rectal prolapse; sphincteroplasty repairs the muscle; a colostomy diverts stool.
sections.body:
When basic care doesn't help, your slides list three options.

Rectal prolapse: apply sugar. Part of the rectum slides out through the anus and can swell. Swollen tissue is hard to push back in. Plain table sugar on the tissue works by osmosis. It pulls water out, the swelling shrinks, and the provider can gently push it back in. It is a simple bedside step used per provider direction. Surgical repair is the long-term fix if it keeps happening.

Anal sphincteroplasty repairs a damaged sphincter, often torn during childbirth, so it can close tightly. It is a surgery specifically for fecal incontinence.

Colostomy sends stool out through a stoma on the belly into a pouch. For severe incontinence nothing else controls, it can restore predictability and dignity. If a client reacts with strong emotion to the idea, reflect the feeling and explore the concern before teaching.
sections.analogy: Sugar on a prolapse works like sugar on sliced strawberries. Soon the berries sit in their own juice, because sugar pulled water out. Swollen tissue gives up its extra water the same way.

check.q: Why is sugar applied to a swollen rectal prolapse?
check.a: Sugar draws fluid out of the swollen tissue by osmosis. The swelling shrinks, so the prolapse can be gently pushed back in.

sections.heading: How do you assess bowel control?
sections.keyIdea: Watch for hidden clues, ask directly but kindly, and examine the abdomen and perianal skin.
sections.body:
Clients rarely say, 'I have fecal incontinence.' The nurse picks up clues. Elimination problems need more direct questions than other topics, because clients are shy to bring them up. Normalize it first: 'Many people have trouble controlling gas or stool. Has that happened to you?'

The concept slides remind you to listen to bowel sounds before you palpate. Touching the belly can change bowel activity.
bullets: Observe: frequent requests for bathroom breaks, fecal odor, soiled clothing, and a client who seems distracted or anxious.
Interview: the extent, onset, and duration. How often, how much, gas or stool, and since when?
History and lifestyle: births, surgeries, nerve or bowel disease, family history, exercise, diet, fluids, thinking, BMI, and smoking.
Abdomen: listen to bowel sounds, then palpate. A firm, tender belly can mean retained stool.
Perianal exam: look for hemorrhoids, fissures, and skin breakdown. A DRE checks sphincter tone and stool, per role and policy.
sections.example: During an admission interview, a 60-year-old client goes to the bathroom three times in 30 minutes and keeps glancing at the door. The nurse kindly asks about bowel control in private. She shares she has had accidents since a hard delivery years ago and has stopped seeing friends. The nurse documents onset and frequency, checks her skin, asks about smoking and diet, and notes the isolation as a problem.

sections.heading: Which problems and goals fit?
sections.keyIdea: Name the nursing problems, then write client-centered goals with a clear result and a number or time.
sections.body:
Your slides list these nursing problems for bowel changes: fecal incontinence, constipation, impaired GI motility, diarrhea, inability to toilet, impaired skin integrity, and low self-esteem. Liquid stool contains enzymes and bacteria that break skin down quickly.

Set priorities with ABCs and safety. With diarrhea and incontinence, signs of fluid loss come first. Open skin comes before psychosocial needs.

Planning is client-centered. Goals are set with the client. Each names the client, an observable result, and a number or time frame. 'Client will have better bowels' can't be measured. The slide goals below can.
bullets: Client will have a soft, formed BM within 4 hours of receiving a laxative.
Client will have a soft, formed stool 3 times per week.
Client will list 4 foods high in fiber.
Client will engage in regular exercise.
Client will maintain perineal hygiene (intact perianal skin).
Client will identify strategies to maintain social interactions.

check.q: Rewrite this goal to be measurable: 'Client will understand fiber.'
check.a: For example: 'Client will list 4 foods high in fiber before discharge.'

sections.heading: What does daily care look like?
sections.keyIdea: Protect the skin after every episode, toilet on a schedule, and protect the client's dignity.
sections.body:
These actions come from the problem list and the concept slides' nurse-led care: fiber and fluid, bowel training, pelvic floor exercises, and hygiene. Clean the client promptly after each episode. Waiting for a scheduled check lets stool damage the skin.

Do not limit fluids for a client with loose stool. Help clients stay social with planning: toilet before leaving, know where restrooms are, and carry a change of clothes.
bullets: Skin: cleanse gently with a pH-balanced cleanser, pat dry, and apply a moisture barrier. Inspect perianal and sacral skin every shift.
Bowel training: offer the toilet at the same time daily, often 20–30 minutes after a meal, to use the gastrocolic reflex.
Stool: use fiber and fluid for soft, formed stool.
Strength: teach Kegel exercises.
Access: call light in reach, fast response, bedside commode, and clothing that is easy to remove.
Dignity: use calm, kind words. Never scold. Say 'briefs' or 'protective underwear,' not 'diapers.'

sections.heading: How do you evaluate the plan?
sections.keyIdea: A goal is met only when the data match every part of it; if it is not met, find out why first.
sections.body: Evaluation asks, did the plan work? Compare the data with every part of the goal. Your slides add a key rule: explore the reasons goals are not met before changing the plan. Do not just swap in a new treatment or lower the goal. Find and fix what got in the way. Your textbook's Patient Teaching: Fecal Elimination (p. 358) can help.
bullets: Have bowel habits improved?
Are fluid intake and diet right?
Is the activity level right?
What obstacles exist? Examples: cost of fresh food, poor teeth, no help, or a new constipating medicine.
Were enough teaching and support given?
sections.example: A goal of 'soft, formed stool 3 times per week' was not met. Before adding a laxative, the nurse asks why. The client stopped eating her high-fiber cereal because her dentures hurt. She also drinks very little to avoid bladder leaks. The real fixes are a dental referral, softer high-fiber foods, and spacing fluids through the day.

check.q: What should the nurse do first when a bowel goal is not met?
check.a: Explore why: diet, fluids, activity, obstacles, and teaching and support. Then change the plan to fix the obstacle found.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Don't confuse impaction seepage with incontinence, or comfort with priority.
sections.body: These look-alikes trip up many students.

rows: Partial vs. major
Partial: gas or minor soiling. Major: can't control normal stool.
True incontinence vs. impaction seepage
Seepage: liquid, no formed stool for days, constipating drugs, rectal pain. Check for impaction.
Sphincteroplasty vs. colostomy
Sphincteroplasty repairs the muscle. A colostomy diverts stool to a pouch.
Cognitive cause vs. weak sphincter
Dementia with normal tone needs scheduled toileting, not sphincter exercises.
Goal not met: change plan vs. explore
Explore the reason first, then fix that obstacle.
Skin vs. emotions: which first?
Fluid loss, then open skin, then psychosocial needs.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect items on hidden clues, measurable goals, priority setting, and the 'explore first' rule.
sections.body:
Common patterns: spot hidden incontinence, choose a measurable goal, set priorities, and evaluate. Red-flag items appear too. New fecal incontinence with new back pain or leg weakness suggests spinal cord compression.

Sample: Which goal is best for a client with fecal incontinence? (A) Client will have better bowel control. (B) Client will have a soft, formed stool 3 times per week. (C) Nurse will teach about fiber. (D) Client will understand the bowel program.
steps: Read the stem: it asks for the best goal statement.
What is it really asking? Which goal is client-centered and measurable?
Key cues: a good goal names the client, an observable result, and a number or time.
Why the others are wrong: A has no measure. C is a nurse action, not a client goal. D uses 'understand,' which can't be observed.
The answer is B. It names the client, the result, and how often.
Reusable strategy: pick goals you could check with your eyes and a number.

sections.heading: Worked case: diarrhea, skin, and shame
sections.keyIdea: Treat the most dangerous problem first, then the skin, then the emotional needs.
sections.body: Mrs. Q, 74, has infectious diarrhea and is incontinent of liquid stool 8 times today. She is dizzy when she stands, and her mouth is dry. Her perianal skin is red and open in one spot. She cries and says, 'I'm so ashamed. I'm like a baby.'
steps: Recognize cues: frequent liquid stool, dizziness, dry mouth, open skin, and distress.
Analyze: the cause is infection. Dizziness and dry mouth suggest fluid loss.
Prioritize: fluid volume deficit first. Report it, monitor vital signs, and support fluids. Do not limit fluids.
Next, the skin: clean promptly after each episode, pat dry, apply a barrier, and inspect every shift.
Then dignity: use calm words, say 'briefs,' not 'diapers,' and let her talk about her feelings.
Evaluate: steady vital signs, healing skin, and fewer episodes as the infection is treated.

check.q: Why does fluid loss come before her emotional distress?
check.a: Fluid loss can quickly become unsafe, causing falls and low blood pressure. Physical safety needs come first, then skin, then psychosocial needs.

pearls: Fecal incontinence is a symptom of another problem and is NOT a normal change of aging.
Partial = gas or minor soiling. Major = can't control stool of normal consistency.
Before labeling a client 'incontinent of liquid stool,' rule out impaction with seepage.
Rectal prolapse plus sugar: osmosis pulls fluid from swollen tissue so the prolapse can be reduced.
Goals must be measurable. If one is not met, find out why before changing the plan.
redFlags: New fecal incontinence with new back pain, leg weakness or numbness, or loss of bladder control: possible spinal cord compression. Report it at once.
Red, weeping, or open perianal or sacral skin: impaired skin integrity is developing. Step up cleansing and barrier care, and report per wound-care protocol.
A prolapsed rectum that turns dark red, purple, or black, or is very painful: its blood supply may be cut off. Notify the provider urgently.

checks.q: A client can't hold gas and has occasional staining but controls formed stool. Partial or major?
checks.a: Partial: unable to control gas or prevent minor soiling.

checks.q: List four risk factors for fecal incontinence from the slides.
checks.a: Advanced age, female sex, smoking, and being overweight or obese (high BMI).

checks.q: Which surgery repairs the muscle that keeps the anus closed?
checks.a: Anal sphincteroplasty.

checks.q: Name three observation clues that suggest a client may have fecal incontinence.
checks.a: Any three: frequent bathroom requests, fecal odor, soiled clothing, and seeming distracted or anxious.

checks.q: Why is 'low self-esteem' on the problem list?
checks.a: Fecal incontinence is distressing and leads to embarrassment and isolation, so the emotional impact is a real nursing problem.
